turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning, Mr Naidoo. Come through, have a seat. How have you been keeping?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Not great, doctor, I'm quite worked up about it. My sugars have been all over the show, and I've had the diabetes fifteen years... no, thirteen years. And now my feet have started tingling.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): All over the show. Tell me what the meter has actually been reading.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, this morning, fasting, it was one-eighty-something. Maybe one-eighty-six, the digits jumped and I couldn't make them out. Is one-eighty dangerous, am I going to land in hospital?
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't act on a number neither of us can read, so we'll do a proper finger-prick here in a moment. Any thirst, or passing a lot of water?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirsty, ja, especially at night. I'm up two or three times. And I'm tired all the time. Is the tiredness just the sugar?
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can be, with sugars running high. Any chest pain, or shortness of breath?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I get a bit puffed climbing the stairs at the flat, but I'm not short of breath when I'm sitting.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the feet, is it both sides?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Both, mostly the toes, pins and needles. It started around Easter... well, actually it was already there in the winter, so four or five months. No pain really. Will I lose the foot, I've seen those pictures online.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): I hear the worry. Any sores, blisters, or a spot that isn't healing?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No sores. I check every night now, I'm that anxious. My wife says I must calm down, but she's at her sister's this week.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Checking is sensible. Eyes now — any blurring, any floaters, or a curtain across the vision?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Blurring, yes, some days, worse when the sugar is high, then it eases off. No floaters, no curtain. When was I meant to have the eye screening? I think I missed the last one.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll come to the screening. Apart from passing more urine at night, any burning when you pass water, or trouble with the bowels?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No burning when I wee. Bowels are fine, no runs or anything.

[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me play that back. Thirteen years of diabetes, thirst, up at night, tingling in both feet for four or five months, blurring on and off, no sores and no chest pain. Now the medicines — tablets and insulin?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Metformin. I was on five hundred twice a day... no, sorry, they put it up, it's a thousand milligrams twice a day, breakfast and supper. About a year on that dose.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): And you actually swallow it every day?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): The metformin, yes, I don't miss that one. The insulin is where I slip.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which insulin, and how many units?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Lantus, the long-acting one, at bedtime. I draw up eighteen units. Um, the sister wrote something different on the card, I think, but I use eighteen.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): The sister's note from last month says twenty-four units of Lantus at night. That is not eighteen. What are you injecting?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Eighteen. I'm sure of eighteen. Twenty-four felt like too much, so I never went up. Is that bad, have I messed the whole thing up?
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): We treat it as not agreed, and I am not changing the pen today. Do you inject every single night?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Not every night. On shift days — I drive the delivery bakkie, those early starts — I skip the evening dose, I'm scared of going low on the road. Maybe three, four nights a week. Is that why the readings are rubbish?
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): It is very likely part of it. Skipping the long-acting insulin can push the sugar up, and it is not a safe way to avoid a low. Was there another tablet?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Gliclazide, eighty milligrams in the morning. I stopped it in March after those hypos at work. Haven't touched it since.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stopped, noted. And the empagliflozin, the Jardiance ten milligrams — did you ever start that?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Never took it. Chemist was out of stock, and then I just never went back. So that one doesn't count, hey?
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then it stays off the list. Any allergies to medicines, rashes, swelling?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing I know of, no rashes or swelling.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): In the family, diabetes or heart trouble?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): My mother had type two, and she lost a toe, that's why I'm panicking. My dad had a heart attack in his sixties.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm sorry, that sits heavy. It raises our attention, it doesn't mean you are on the same path. Do you smoke, or take alcohol?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Stopped smoking twelve years back. A beer on a Saturday, maybe two, nothing in the week.

[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll take the observations. Blood pressure is one hundred and forty-eight over ninety... sorry, reading it properly, one hundred and fifty-two over ninety-four. Pulse is eighty-two... no, seventy-six.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that high? Should I be on a blood pressure tablet? My brother takes one and he's fine.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's up a bit today, and I'm not starting a tablet off one reading. Finger-prick glucose is eleven point six millimoles per litre. Not a crisis, but higher than we want. Shoes off, please, I'll look at the feet.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): They're a bit dry, hey. Is dry skin dangerous? I keep thinking every mark is the start of something.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Skin is intact on both feet, no ulcers, no open cracks. Pulses are present in both feet. With the monofilament, sensation is reduced over the toes on both sides, which fits the tingling.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): So it is the nerves? If I get the sugar right, does it come back? Please don't soften it.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working impression is type two diabetes that is not well controlled, with early peripheral neuropathy. I can't promise the tingling will disappear, but better sugars usually stop it marching on. Your tummy injection sites look fine, no lumps.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. What do I actually do about eighteen versus twenty-four? And can I still drive the bakkie, or is that finished?

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stay on eighteen units at night, the dose you have been taking, until the diabetes sister reconciles the card. Don't jump to twenty-four on your own. Driving is all right if you are not hypo — keep glucose sweets in the bakkie.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): And the metformin, my stomach rumbles on it sometimes. Should I just stop it?

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't stop it. Take it in the middle of the meal, not on an empty stomach. If it turns into proper runs we'll rethink, but not today. I'm sending an HbA1c, kidney function, and a urine sample for protein.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): When does all that happen? Do I have to come back fasting another day? I can't keep taking leave.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): No, the sister can draw them before you leave today, so they're booked. And I'm referring you for retinal screening, since you missed the last one.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. How soon will they call? And do I need those special shoes, the expensive ones?

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): The referral goes today; the eye clinic sends the date, I don't have it yet. Shoes: well-fitting closed shoes, no barefoot around the house, check the feet every night. Moisturise the dry skin, but not between the toes.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): If the tingling gets worse before I see you, or I spot a sore, do I wait the month or come in?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back sooner if you get a sore, a hot red foot, chest pain, or a hypo you can't sort out yourself. Otherwise I'll see you in four weeks with the results.

[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks, shame, I hope it's not a disaster. Oh, completely off the point, did you catch the Proteas last night, that last over, I nearly fell off the couch. And the N1 this morning was a mess, robots out from the load shedding. Took me an hour just from Midrand, the bakkie crawling the whole way.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): I saw the highlights, that catch at midwicket was lovely. The N1 never does anyone a favour in the morning. It doesn't change what we're doing today, though.

[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, sorry, I talk when I'm nervous. So, just so I don't get it wrong — eighteen units, try not to skip, metformin a thousand twice a day, bloods today, eyes referral, back in four weeks?

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's the summary. Eighteen units nightly until we reconcile the card, please try not to skip it on shift days, metformin one thousand milligrams twice a day with food, bloods and urine today, retinal screening referral, and a review here in four weeks. Anything else sitting on you?
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): If I feel low at work I stop and I eat, I don't push through. Thank you, doctor. I'll try to keep the panic down.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

bad.reason: Retinal screening referral and missed last screening are stated; transcript does not call it imaging.
bad.text: retinal screening (type=imaging, status=planned, requested_by=doctor, indication=missed the last screening)

omissions.text: Lantus dose is incompletely recorded under medications: the patient reported injecting 18 units at bedtime/nightly (despite a conflicting card saying 24 units).
The patient is not taking Lantus every night; he skips the evening dose on shift days about 3 to 4 nights per week because he is afraid of going low while driving.
Empagliflozin (Jardiance) 10 mg was never started because the chemist was out of stock and the patient never went back; it should remain off the medication list.
Negative finding missing: no shortness of breath when sitting, despite being a bit puffed on stairs.
Negative finding missing: no blisters on the feet.
Negative finding missing: bowels fine with no diarrhoea/runs was specifically asked and answered.
Allergy history is incompletely recorded: the patient denied medication allergies and specifically denied rashes or swelling.
Physical examination omission: skin intact on both feet.
Physical examination omission: no open cracks in either foot.
Planned investigations timing missing: HbA1c, kidney function tests, and urine protein were to be drawn before the patient leaves today (not on a later fasting visit).
The patient had missed the last retinal screening / thought he missed the last eye screening.
Additional counselling/safety advice missing: driving is acceptable if he is not hypoglycaemic.
Additional counselling about metformin missing: if it turns into proper diarrhoea/runs they will rethink it, but not today.
The patient reported self-management advice for hypoglycaemia: if he feels low at work, he stops and eats rather than pushing through.
